raw_case_text:
A 28-year-old Sri Lankan male residing in the Middle East was admitted with high-grade fever (102-104 F) with chills, night sweats, progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, malaise, loss of appetite, and unintentional loss of weight (11 kg) for 1 month, after returning to Sri Lanka. He has been previously well and denied active or passive smoking. His mother had pulmonary tuberculosis 15 years ago. He had been well during contact tracing at that time and his Tuberculin skin test (Mantoux) had been negative.
He was ill-looking, pale, febrile, and dyspneic with peripheral oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Mobile, non-matted small lymph nodes were palpable in the left anterior triangle of the neck and bilateral inguinal regions. Chest examination suggested possible bilateral pleural effusions, while abdominal examination found hepatomegaly of 2 cm and mild splenomegaly. These findings were confirmed with a bedside ultrasound scan.
Chest x-ray showed moderate right and small left pleural effusions and <5 mm tiny nodules affecting all zones (Figure 1). Subsequent Computed tomography scans of chest and abdomen revealed bilateral pleural effusion (right > left), multiple nodules mainly involving posterior, basal, and apical segments of the right lower lobe, and posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly without evidence of ascites or para-aortic lymph nodes.
His Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 9 mm/h, C reactive protein 28.9 mg/L, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, had mild neutrophil leukocytosis (White cell count 11.6 x 103/uL, neutrophils 90%, lymphocytes 10%), platelets 399 x 103/microL. Liver enzymes were mildly elevated (Aspartate transaminase 64 U/L, Alanine transaminase 55 U/L) and serum creatinine was normal (70.4 micromol/L).
The patient underwent therapeutic needle aspiration of approximately 550 ml of milky white pleural fluid on the right side. It was exudative with lymphocytic predominance (WBC count 3440, RBC 1600, polymorphs 18, lymphocytes 82, pleural protein level 3.69 g/dL, sugar 151 mg/dL). Pleural triglyceride (TG) was 1374 mg/dL, pleural total cholesterol was 70 mg/dL, and pleural Lactate dehydrogenase was 432 U/L. Serum TG was 137 mg/dL (pleural fluid: serum TG = 10) and cholesterol was 156 mg/dL (pleural fluid: serum cholesterol = 0.44). The serum LDH count was 386 U/L. Pleural fluid was negative for atypical cells and bacterial growth. Pleural fluid for Adenosine diaminase was 27.7 IU. Antibodies for melioidosis and HIV were negative.
A diagnosis of disseminated/miliary tuberculosis complicated with bilateral chylothorax was made on high clinical suspicion with biochemical and radiological evidence, and the patient was started on Anti tuberculous therapy according to the National Guidelines for Tuberculosis Control (2021)   on Day 06 of admission. To confirm the diagnosis, pleural fluid TB PCR (tuberculosis polymerase chain reaction), sputum for Acid fast bacilli and TB PCR was done, which was negative. Sputum for TB culture was sent. The patient's Mantoux test became positive with 18 mm induration after 48 h. Due to cervical lymph nodes being small (0.5-1 cm), a biopsy could not be done.
The patient's symptoms persisted with oxygen dependency despite pleural aspiration and continuation of ATT, and serial bedside ultrasound scans of the chest confirmed recurring bilateral moderate pleural effusions, which warranted bilateral intercostal tube insertions on Days 12 and 16 of admission for continuous pleural drainage. Both intercostal tubes tubes drained 300-700 ml/day per side for approximately 21 days, after which the drainage gradually subsided, and the tubes were removed on Day 28. During the intense period, he was provided with a high-calorie, low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride-containing diet, chest physiotherapy, and mobilization advice to prevent thromboembolism.
Meanwhile, a diagnostic thoracoscopy was performed on Day 15 (Figure 2), which revealed densely inflamed parietal and visceral pleurae and enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes with caseous discharge. Biopsies taken from the parietal pleura and mediastinal nodes showed inflamed pleural tissue and xanthogranulomatous lymphadenitis.
The patient was discharged on Day 32 of ATT, and his sputum culture became positive for M. tuberculosis at 6 weeks of incubation, confirming the diagnosis of tuberculosis. At the 2-month review, the patient had much improved symptomatically, and the ultrasound scan was negative for pleural effusions. ATT continuation phase was extended to 10 months for disseminated TB.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 28-year-old Sri Lankan male presented with a 1-month history of high-grade fever, chills, night sweats, progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, malaise, anorexia, and an 11 kg unintentional weight loss.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient developed high-grade fever (102-104 F) with chills, night sweats, progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, malaise, loss of appetite, and unintentional weight loss of 11 kg over 1 month after returning to Sri Lanka from the Middle East.
subjective.past_medical_history: Previously well; resided in the Middle East before returning to Sri Lanka; denied active or passive smoking. Family history was notable for pulmonary tuberculosis in his mother 15 years earlier, during which he remained well on contact tracing with a negative Mantoux tuberculin skin test.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for high-grade fever, chills, night sweats, progressive dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, malaise, anorexia, and 11 kg weight loss.

objective.physical_examination: Ill-looking, pale, febrile, and dyspneic with peripheral oxygen saturation of 90% on room air. Mobile, non-matted small lymph nodes (0.5-1 cm) were palpable in the left anterior triangle of the neck and bilateral inguinal regions. Chest examination suggested bilateral pleural effusions, and abdominal examination revealed 2 cm hepatomegaly and mild splenomegaly.
objective.routine_investigations: Bedside ultrasound confirmed bilateral pleural effusions, hepatomegaly, and splenomegaly. Chest X-ray showed moderate right and small left pleural effusions with <5 mm tiny nodules across all lung zones. Laboratory results: ESR 9 mm/h, CRP 28.9 mg/L, hemoglobin 10.8 g/dL, WBC 11.6 x 10^3/uL (neutrophils 90%, lymphocytes 10%), platelets 399 x 10^3/microL, AST 64 U/L, ALT 55 U/L, serum creatinine 70.4 micromol/L, serum triglycerides 137 mg/dL, serum total cholesterol 156 mg/dL, and serum LDH 386 U/L. Mantoux test became positive with 18 mm induration at 48 hours.
objective.advanced_workup: CT chest and abdomen revealed bilateral pleural effusions (right > left), multiple pulmonary nodules mainly in the posterior, basal, and apical segments of the right lower lobe and posterior basal segment of the left lower lobe, bilateral hilar and mediastinal lymphadenopathy, and hepatosplenomegaly without ascites or para-aortic lymphadenopathy. Right thoracentesis yielded 550 mL of milky white exudative chylous fluid: WBC 3440 (polymorphs 18%, lymphocytes 82%), RBC 1600, protein 3.69 g/dL, sugar 151 mg/dL, pleural triglycerides 1374 mg/dL (pleural:serum TG ratio = 10), pleural total cholesterol 70 mg/dL (pleural:serum cholesterol ratio = 0.44), pleural LDH 432 U/L, adenosine deaminase (ADA) 27.7 IU, and negative cytology and bacterial culture. Pleural fluid TB PCR, sputum acid-fast bacilli (AFB) smear, and sputum TB PCR were negative. Antibodies for melioidosis and HIV were negative. Day 15 diagnostic thoracoscopy showed densely inflamed parietal and visceral pleurae and enlarged hilar and mediastinal lymph nodes with caseous discharge; biopsies demonstrated inflamed pleural tissue and xanthogranulomatous lymphadenitis.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis: Disseminated/miliary tuberculosis complicated by bilateral chylothorax, definitively confirmed when sputum culture grew Mycobacterium tuberculosis at 6 weeks of incubation (melioidosis and HIV were ruled out by negative serologies). Management and course: Anti-tuberculous therapy (ATT) was initiated on day 6 of admission per National Guidelines. Due to recurring bilateral moderate chylous effusions and persistent oxygen dependency, bilateral intercostal chest tubes were inserted on days 12 and 16 (draining 300-700 mL/day per side for ~21 days before removal on day 28), supported by a high-calorie, low-fat, medium-chain triglyceride diet, chest physiotherapy, and mobilization. He was discharged on day 32 of ATT, showed marked symptomatic improvement and no residual effusion on ultrasound at the 2-month review, and had his ATT continuation phase extended to 10 months.
